There's a particular quality to the moment a kettle begins to boil that I find myself returning to. Not the whistle or the click of the switch, but the seconds just before—when the water shifts from silence to a low, uneven murmur, as if it's clearing its throat. Small bubbles form at the bottom, rise, and collapse before reaching the surface. Physicists call this the onset of nucleate boiling. I call it the sound of something making up its mind.

What strikes me is how much happens in that interval that nobody watches. We fill the kettle and walk away. We check our phones, glance out the window, think about the day's small obligations. Meanwhile, an entire drama of phase transition plays out in the dark of a steel cylinder: energy pouring in, molecules gaining speed, order dissolving into disorder in the most ordinary way imaginable.

I think there's something worth noticing here about attention. So much of what we call "waiting" is actually a refusal to look. The kettle isn't idle; we are. And the same is true of bread rising, of paint drying, of a friendship slowly changing shape over months. The transformation is constant. It's only our gaze that's intermittent.

I don't mean this as a lecture on mindfulness. I'm as guilty as anyone of drifting off during the murmur. But every so often I stand there and listen, and the ordinary becomes briefly astonishing—water becoming steam, patience becoming tea, a small daily miracle that asks for nothing except that someone occasionally notice it happening.
